promptHead: Athlete goal: marathon (Wexley Lakes Marathon) on Sun Nov 1 2026, 6 weeks out, target under 3:45.

new.headline: You turned a corner, then jumped two steps at once; next week pulls back on purpose so the gains stick instead of turning into an injury.

flags.title: Overload warning
flags.detail: your weekly effort score (423) was nearly double the three-week average (223), and that jump is where injuries usually show up.

flags.title: Plan overrun across the week
flags.detail: every planned run grew, including a surprise Monday run and a fourth threshold rep, so almost nothing matched what we agreed.

flags.title: Long run too hard
flags.detail: 20 mi at an average heart rate of 149 put 88 percent of the run in zone 3, not the easy zone we wanted.

flags.title: Easy share only 54 percent
flags.detail: well below the 80 percent target because the long run and threshold both tipped into harder zones.

flags.title: Calves tight Sunday night
flags.detail: a small signal after that long run, so I want to see it clear this week before we push again.

answers.question: I ran way more than the plan and felt fine. Can I keep this up?
answers.answer: No, please do not keep this up. You felt fine in the moment, but weekly mileage went from about 30 to 37 to 53 in three weeks, and that is roughly a 40 percent jump two weeks running. The body tends to send the bill a week or two later as a tight calf, a cranky knee, or a tendon that will not settle, and you already have a note about tight calves on Sunday night. The smarter plan is to hold the shape of the week I give you (one quality session, one long run, the rest easy) and let fitness compound week over week. Six weeks out from the race, the goal is to arrive healthy and sharp, not to prove you can run more. If a run feels great, bank that feeling and use it in the quality session or the next long run, not by stacking extra miles on an easy day.

new.analysis:
The reviewed week was a strong week of running wrapped around a risky pattern. You added a Monday run, pushed every easy day longer, added a fourth threshold rep at 7:55/mi, and extended the long run from 15 mi to 20 mi. Any one of those is a reasonable call on a good day; all four in one week is how good training weeks become bad injury weeks.

The long run is the piece I most want to change. You held 10:02/mi, which looks easy on paper, but your heart rate sat at 149 and 88 percent of the time was in zone 3. For a marathon long run at this stage I want zone 2 almost the whole way, which for you means closer to 10:20 to 10:40/mi, especially in the first half. Running the long one truly easy is what lets the next workout land properly.

Next week is a small cutback on purpose. We drop total miles to around 39, bring the long run back to 16 mi fully easy, and introduce a short block at goal marathon pace (8:35/mi for 3:45) in the midweek session so your legs start learning race rhythm. Treat the plan as a ceiling this week, not a floor, and let the calves settle. If next Sunday goes well and easy, we push the long run back up the following week and layer in marathon-pace miles there too.
